The Rock hind (Epinephelus adscensionis) exhibits a suite of life-history traits typical of a moderately long-lived, iteroparous serranid. The newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves as they begin their pelagic larval phase. The initial wet weight at birth, derived from the egg diameter of 0.95 mm, is just 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams], a remarkably small mass that underscores the high fecundity characteristic of this genus. This tiny size at the onset of exogenous feeding imposes substantial challenges, as the larvae must encounter suitably small planktonic prey within the first few days following yolk-sac resorption.

As the pelagic teleost larvae progress through the preflexion and flexion stages, they undergo rapid somatic growth. The ultimate total length recorded for adult Rock hind reaches 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], placing this species among the medium-sized groupers within its genus. Attaining this maximum size requires several years of sustained feeding and reflects the favourable conditions of the subtropical reef environments it inhabits. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual, calculated from the length–weight relationship, reaches approximately 5011 grams [Wwi = approximately 5011 grams]. This size threshold marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence, when individuals begin diverting resources toward reproductive investment. The timing of puberty is influenced by both local food availability and population density, with individuals in lower-quality habitats often delaying maturation until they reach a larger size. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active females, measured at a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], averaged 4% [GSI = 4%] during the peak of the spawning season.

The maximum recorded lifespan for the Rock hind, maintained at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], is approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years], making it one of the more long-lived members of the Epinephelus genus found in the western Atlantic. This longevity is supported by the species slow but steady growth trajectory after reaching sexual maturity, with annual increments in length declining progressively after the first decade of life. Large, old individuals are particularly important for population reproductive output, as they contribute disproportionately to the egg and larval pool due to their greater fecundity. Field surveys from protected areas have documented individuals exceeding 20 years of age, confirming that the species can persist under low fishing mortality. The extended lifespan also provides multiple breeding seasons, allowing the population to buffer against intermittent recruitment failures driven by oceanographic variability.

Females produce multiple clutches per spawning season, with batch fecundity scaling positively with body size; a 475-gram female (475 grams) [Wwp = 475 grams] at first maturity will carry fewer oocytes than a larger, more experienced individual exceeding 5011 grams [Wwi = 5011 grams]. The species is a protogynous hermaphrodite, a reproductive strategy common among groupers, where individuals typically mature first as females and later transition to males after attaining a larger size. This sex change occurs well after individuals surpass 30.4 centimeters [Lp = 30.4 centimeters] in total length, ensuring that the largest, most dominant fish in the population are male. Understanding this life-history pattern is critical for fisheries management, as selective harvest of large males can skew sex ratios and reduce reproductive output.
